National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments 16

  1. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Lincoln Memorial

    Henry Bacon's Doric temple (1922) housing Daniel Chester French's 19-foot seated Lincoln, the terminus of the Reflecting Pool and the spot where Dr. King delivered 'I Have a Dream.' Open 24 hours, free, ranger-staffed.

    Look for memorial

    2 Lincoln Memorial Cir NW, Washington, DC 20037

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  2. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Washington Monument

    The 555-foot marble obelisk (completed 1884) honoring the first president, the tallest structure in DC. Grounds are open daily; the interior elevator to the observation deck has faced repeated closures, so check NPS for current top access before you go.

    Look for monument

    2 15th St NW, Washington, DC 20024

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  3. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Thomas Jefferson Memorial

    John Russell Pope's domed rotunda (1943) on the Tidal Basin, with a 19-foot bronze of Jefferson ringed by his own words. One of the finest cherry-blossom vantage points each spring.

    Look for memorial

    16 E Basin Dr SW, Washington, DC 20242

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  4. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    National World War II Memorial

    A plaza of 56 granite pillars and two arches around a fountain between the Washington Monument and the Reflecting Pool, dedicated 2004 to the 16 million who served. The Freedom Wall bears 4,048 gold stars.

    Look for memorial

    1750 Independence Ave SW, Washington, DC 20024

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  5. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Vietnam Veterans Memorial

    Maya Lin's stark black-granite wall (1982) inscribed with the 58,000-plus names of the fallen and missing, sunk into the earth beside the Three Soldiers statue. Among the most-visited and most-moving sites on the Mall.

    Look for memorial

    5 Henry Bacon Dr NW, Washington, DC 20037

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  6. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial

    A 30-foot 'Stone of Hope' likeness of Dr. King emerging from a split boulder on the Tidal Basin's northwest rim, opened 2011. A 450-foot inscription wall carries 14 of his quotations.

    Look for memorial

    1964 Independence Ave SW, Washington, DC 20024

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  7. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    National Gallery of Art

    The nation's art museum (not a Smithsonian), pairing John Russell Pope's neoclassical West Building with I.M. Pei's East Building, plus a sculpture garden. Free; home to the only Leonardo da Vinci in the Americas.

    Look for museum

    6th St & Constitution Ave NW, Washington, DC 20565

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  8. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    National Air and Space Museum

    The Smithsonian's flagship of flight and spaceflight, home to the Wright Flyer, Spirit of St. Louis, and Apollo 11 command module. Reopened in full for its 50th anniversary in July 2026 after a multi-year renovation; free, timed passes recommended.

    Look for museum

    655 Jefferson Dr SW, Washington, DC 20560

    Recommended by Smithsonian Institution

  9. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    National Museum of Natural History

    The Smithsonian's natural-history giant, home to the Hope Diamond, a live butterfly pavilion, dinosaurs and the Ocean Hall. Free admission, one of the most-visited museums on earth.

    Look for museum

    10th St & Constitution Ave NW, Washington, DC 20560

    Recommended by Smithsonian Institution

  10. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    National Museum of American History

    Keeper of the original Star-Spangled Banner, the Ruby Slippers, Julia Child's kitchen and the First Ladies' gowns. A free Smithsonian survey of the American story.

    Look for museum

    1300 Constitution Ave NW, Washington, DC 20560

    Recommended by Smithsonian Institution

  11. Must see · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    National Museum of African American History and Culture

    David Adjaye's bronze-corona building (opened 2016), the Smithsonian's newest and among its most sought-after, tracing slavery through the present across culture, sport and struggle. Free, but timed passes are advised.

    Look for museum

    1400 Constitution Ave NW, Washington, DC 20560

    Recommended by Smithsonian Institution

  12. Worth the detour · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Korean War Veterans Memorial

    Nineteen stainless-steel soldiers advance through juniper toward an American flag, mirrored on a granite wall to read as 38 (the 38th parallel). The 2022 Wall of Remembrance added the names of the dead.

    Look for memorial

    10 Daniel French Dr SW, Washington, DC 20024

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  13. Worth the detour · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial

    A 7.5-acre sequence of four granite outdoor 'rooms,' one per FDR term, threaded with waterfalls, sculpture and quotations. Opened 1997 on the Tidal Basin's Cherry Tree Walk.

    Look for memorial

    1850 West Basin Dr SW, Washington, DC 20242

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  14. Worth the detour · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Tidal Basin & the Cherry Blossoms

    The man-made inlet ringed by the Jefferson, FDR and MLK memorials and by 3,000-plus Yoshino cherry trees, a 1912 gift from Tokyo that draws peak-bloom crowds each late March. Paddleboats and a walking loop year-round.

    Look for waterfront

    1501 Maine Ave SW, Washington, DC 20024

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  15. Worth the detour · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    United States Botanic Garden

    A living plant museum at the foot of Capitol Hill, its 1933 glass Conservatory holding a jungle, orchids and a seasonal garden-railway show. Free, and one of the oldest continually operating botanic gardens in the country.

    Look for garden

    100 Maryland Ave SW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  16. Worth the detour · National Mall, Tidal Basin & the Monuments

    Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden

    The Smithsonian's modern and contemporary art museum, a cylindrical 'donut' by Gordon Bunshaft with a sunken sculpture garden across Jefferson Drive. Free; strong in Rothko, Bourgeois and immersive installations.

    Look for museum

    Independence Ave SW & 7th St SW, Washington, DC 20560

    Recommended by Smithsonian Institution

Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown 15

  1. Must see · Chinese, Thai, Japanese & More · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Daikaya

    The restaurant that introduced DC to serious ramen (2013): a Sapporo-style ramen bar downstairs with noodles handcrafted and imported from Japan, and a full izakaya upstairs, from chef Katsuya Fukushima. A perennial Eater essential; The Infatuation and Gayot both rate it a Chinatown/Penn Quarter must, and there's usually a line.

    705 6th St NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by INFATUATION, GAYOT, TIMEOUT

  2. Must see · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    The White House

    The executive mansion and workplace of every president since John Adams, viewable from Lafayette Square and the south Ellipse. Interior tours are free but must be arranged well ahead through a member of Congress.

    Look for landmark

    1600 Pennsylvania Ave NW, Washington, DC 20500

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  3. Must see · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    National Archives Museum

    Home of the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, displayed in the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom. Free admission.

    Look for landmark

    701 Constitution Ave NW, Washington, DC 20408

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  4. Must see · American, New American & Steak · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Rania

    One Michelin star — chef Chetan Shetty (ex-Indian Accent) reinvents Indian fine dining in a regal Penn Quarter room; the Washington Post calls it adventurous Indian cooking in a regal setting. Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.

    427 11th St NW, Washington, DC 20004

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, The Washington Post

  5. Must see · American, New American & Steak · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Fiola

    One Michelin star — Fabio Trabocchi's luxe downtown Italian, a longtime power-dining room off Pennsylvania Avenue. Holds its star in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide Washington, D.C.

    601 Pennsylvania Ave NW, Washington, DC 20004

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, Wikipedia

  6. Must see · American, New American & Steak · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Rasika

    DC's most acclaimed Indian restaurant — Ashok Bajaj's Penn Quarter icon, whose crackling palak chaat is a citywide signature; a MICHELIN Guide recommended pick and a perennial Washingtonian 100 Very Best.

    633 D St NW, Washington, DC 20004

    Recommended by MICHELIN, WASHINGTONIAN

  7. Must see · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Smithsonian American Art Museum & National Portrait Gallery

    Two free Smithsonian museums sharing the Greek Revival Old Patent Office Building in Penn Quarter, joined by the glass-roofed Kogod Courtyard. The Portrait Gallery's 'America's Presidents' is the only complete set outside the White House.

    Look for museum

    800 G St NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by Smithsonian Institution

  8. Worth the detour · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Ford's Theatre

    The still-operating 1863 theater where Lincoln was shot on April 14, 1865, now an NPS site with a museum and the Petersen House (where he died) across the street. Working stage plus historical tours.

    Look for historic

    511 10th St NW, Washington, DC 20004

    Recommended by National Park Service, Official site / operator

  9. Worth the detour · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    National Building Museum

    A soaring 1887 Great Hall lined with 75-foot Corinthian columns, once the Pension Bureau, now devoted to architecture, design and engineering. Known for blockbuster summer installations; the Great Hall is free.

    Look for museum

    401 F St NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  10. Worth the detour · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    International Spy Museum

    A privately run, glass-clad museum of espionage at L'Enfant Plaza, with one of the largest public collections of spy artifacts and interactive tradecraft exhibits. Ticketed admission.

    Look for museum

    700 L'Enfant Plaza SW, Washington, DC 20024

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  11. Worth the detour · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Chinatown Friendship Archway

    A 75-foot, seven-roof gate over H Street (1986), the largest single-span Chinese archway of its kind, marking the entrance to DC's compact Chinatown near Capital One Arena.

    Look for landmark

    610 H St NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by Destination DC (washington.org), Atlas Obscura

  12. Worth the detour · Chesapeake Seafood & Raw Bars · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Old Ebbitt Grill

    A block from the White House, DC's oldest saloon (1856) runs one of the city's busiest raw bars and its annual Oyster Riot. A tourist-and-lobbyist institution whose oysters on the half shell and crab cakes make it a dependable Chesapeake stop downtown.

    675 15th St NW, Washington, DC 20005

    Recommended by Destination DC (washington.org), USA TODAY 10BEST

  13. Worth the detour · South Asian & Afghan · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    Bombay Club

    Ashok Bajaj's first DC restaurant (1989), a genteel colonial-era dining room a block from the White House long favored by presidents and cabinet secretaries. A Washingtonian mainstay whose refined North Indian cooking helped set the template for the city's upscale Indian scene.

    815 Connecticut Ave NW, Washington, DC 20006

    Recommended by WASHINGTONIAN, Official site / operator

  14. Worth the detour · American, New American & Steak · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    L'Ardente

    MICHELIN Bib Gourmand — chef John Manolatos's glam East End Italian, whose viral 40-layer lasagna became a citywide sensation. Named a Bib Gourmand in the MICHELIN Guide Washington, D.C.

    200 Massachusetts Ave NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by MICHELIN BIB GOURMAND, Wikipedia

  15. Worth the detour · West & Sub-Saharan African · Downtown, Penn Quarter & Chinatown

    The Continent DC

    DC's upscale West African flagship (opened 2024) from Nigerian-American founder Ope Amosu, a 175-seat downtown room built around a Nigerian core — egusi, bitterleaf (ofe onugbu), beef suya, Lagos snapper — that shifts to a lounge scene on weekends. Reviewed by The Infatuation and featured in Destination DC's dining coverage; fills a real West African gap for a "Chocolate City."

    1110 Vermont Ave NW, Washington, DC 20005

    Recommended by INFATUATION, Destination DC (washington.org)

Georgetown & Foggy Bottom 8

  1. Must see · Georgetown & Foggy Bottom

    John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts

    The nation's living memorial to JFK and its busiest performing-arts complex, on the Potomac beside the Watergate, home to the National Symphony and Washington National Opera. Free daily performances on the Millennium Stage and a rooftop terrace with river views.

    Look for entertainment

    2700 F St NW, Washington, DC 20566

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  2. Must see · Georgetown & Foggy Bottom

    Georgetown Waterfront & the C&O Canal

    The cobblestoned C&O Canal towpath and the Potomac-front park frame Georgetown's shops and rowing crews, with mule-drawn boat history at the NPS canal. A walkable stretch of the neighborhood's 18th-century core.

    Look for waterfront

    3303 Water St NW, Washington, DC 20007

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  3. Must see · Mediterranean & Middle Eastern · Georgetown & Foggy Bottom

    Imperfecto

    One Michelin star — chef Enrique Limardo's Mediterranean-meets-Latin-American cooking in the West End, a chef's-table experience of bold, cross-continental plates. Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.

    1124 23rd St NW, Washington, DC 20037

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, Wikipedia

  4. Must see · Ethiopian & East African · Georgetown & Foggy Bottom

    Das Ethiopian Cuisine

    Ethiopian dining inside a classic Georgetown townhouse — soothing rooms, attentive service that walks newcomers through the menu, and a much-praised doro wot. A MICHELIN Bib Gourmand honoree (2021 onward), a lone institutional authority, and the rare authentic Ethiopian option west of the Little Ethiopia corridor.

    1201 28th St NW, Washington, DC 20007

    Recommended by MICHELIN BIB GOURMAND, WASHINGTONIAN

  5. Worth the detour · Georgetown & Foggy Bottom

    Dumbarton Oaks

    A Harvard-run research estate in upper Georgetown celebrated for its Byzantine and Pre-Columbian art and, above all, Beatrix Farrand's terraced formal gardens. Museum is free; the gardens are ticketed in season.

    Look for garden

    1703 32nd St NW, Washington, DC 20007

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  6. Worth the detour · Georgetown & Foggy Bottom

    Old Stone House

    Built in 1765, the oldest unchanged building in DC and a rare survivor of pre-Revolutionary Georgetown, now an NPS house museum with a colonial-style garden. Free.

    Look for historic

    3051 M St NW, Washington, DC 20007

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  7. Worth the detour · Georgetown & Foggy Bottom

    Georgetown University & Healy Hall

    The oldest Catholic and Jesuit university in the United States (founded 1789), whose Flemish-Romanesque Healy Hall and its clock-tower spires crown the campus above the Potomac. Grounds are open to visitors.

    Look for landmark

    3700 O St NW, Washington, DC 20057

    Recommended by Wikipedia, Destination DC (washington.org)

  8. Worth the detour · Chesapeake Seafood & Raw Bars · Georgetown & Foggy Bottom

    Fiola Mare

    Fabio Trabocchi's glamorous Georgetown waterfront seafood room on the Potomac at Washington Harbour — a Washingtonian 100 Very Best and the marquee special-occasion table on the water.

    3050 K St NW, Washington, DC 20007

    Recommended by WASHINGTONIAN, MICHELIN

Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan 8

  1. Must see · Chinese, Thai, Japanese & More · Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan

    Chang Chang

    Sichuan legend Peter Chang's polished DC flagship, where he applies precision to Sichuan and classic Chinese cooking without dialing down the heat. The Washington Post's Tom Sietsema reviewed it as "worth the wait," Esquire named it a Best New Restaurant (2023), and it carries a MICHELIN Guide listing; The Infatuation is a fan. Peter Chang is a past James Beard finalist.

    1200 19th St NW, Washington, DC 20036

    Recommended by The Washington Post, MICHELIN, INFATUATION

  2. Must see · Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan

    The Phillips Collection

    America's first museum of modern art (1921), an intimate Dupont Circle mansion whose crown jewel is Renoir's 'Luncheon of the Boating Party,' plus a meditative Rothko Room. Ticketed for special exhibitions.

    Look for museum

    1600 21st St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  3. Must see · Chesapeake Seafood & Raw Bars · Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan

    Hank's Oyster Bar

    Chef Jamie Leeds's Dupont original, repeatedly voted DC's best raw bar and seafood restaurant and praised by Washingtonian, Bon Appetit and Food & Wine. The seafood plateau, Maine-style lobster roll and Chesapeake crab cakes headline a menu built around East Coast oysters.

    1624 Q St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by WASHINGTONIAN, Official site / operator

  4. Must see · American, New American & Steak · Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan

    Le Diplomate

    Stephen Starr's landmark Logan Circle brasserie — the see-and-be-seen French cafe that anchored the 14th Street revival; a Washingtonian 100 Very Best and one of DC's hardest tables.

    1601 14th St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by WASHINGTONIAN, Official site / operator

  5. Must see · Chinese, Thai, Japanese & More · Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan

    Sushi Taro

    The city's benchmark for traditional Japanese dining: a MICHELIN-starred kaiseki-and-sushi room above a Dupont Circle CVS, run by second-generation chef Nobu Yamazaki, who reinvented the family restaurant into an upmarket kaiseki house. The MICHELIN star is a lone institutional authority; Time Out ranks it among DC's very best Japanese. Fish is flown from Toyosu.

    1503 17th St NW, Washington, DC 20036

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, TIMEOUT

  6. Worth the detour · Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan

    Embassy Row

    The Massachusetts Avenue stretch northwest of Dupont Circle lined with more than 50 embassies and Gilded Age mansions, marked by statues of Gandhi, Churchill and Mandela. A self-guided architectural walk.

    Look for district

    2300 Massachusetts Ave NW, Washington, DC 20008

    Recommended by Destination DC (washington.org), Wikipedia

  7. Worth the detour · Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan

    Adams Morgan (18th Street)

    DC's most eclectic nightlife-and-dining strip, famous for its murals, international restaurants and the late-night jumbo slice. A lively, walkable neighborhood core.

    Look for district

    18th St NW & Columbia Rd NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by Destination DC (washington.org), Wikipedia

  8. Worth the detour · Dupont, Logan Circle & Adams Morgan

    Dupont Circle & Fountain

    The traffic-circle park at the heart of the neighborhood, its 1921 marble fountain designed by the Lincoln Memorial's team, ringed by bookstores, cafes and a Sunday farmers market. A classic people-watching green.

    Look for district

    1 Dupont Cir NW, Washington, DC 20036

    Recommended by Destination DC (washington.org), Wikipedia

U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights 16

  1. Must see · Burgers, Half-Smokes & Diners · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Ben's Chili Bowl

    The definitive home of DC's signature half-smoke, a U Street institution since 1958. A James Beard Foundation "America's Classics" honoree (2004) and Bon Appetit "Best Chili Spots" pick; the half-smoke — a spicier, coarser pork-and-beef sausage smothered in Ben's chili — is the top seller and a genuine city icon.

    1213 U St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by JAMES BEARD, Destination DC (washington.org), Official site / operator

  2. Must see · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    African American Civil War Memorial & Museum

    A bronze 'Spirit of Freedom' sculpture and a wall inscribed with the 209,000-plus names of the U.S. Colored Troops, paired with a museum around the corner on U Street. Anchors the historic Black cultural heart of the city.

    Look for memorial

    1925 Vermont Ave NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  3. Must see · American, New American & Steak · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Jont

    Two Michelin stars — Ryan Ratino's intimate upstairs tasting counter on 14th Street, DC's only two-star outside minibar and the Inn at Little Washington. Held both stars in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.

    1904 14th St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, Wikipedia

  4. Must see · American, New American & Steak · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Bresca

    One Michelin star — Ryan Ratino's honey-themed 14th Street bistro (below Jont), starred every year since it opened. Retains its star in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide Washington, D.C.

    1906 14th St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, Wikipedia

  5. Must see · American, New American & Steak · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    The Dabney

    One Michelin star — Jeremiah Langhorne's wood-hearth Shaw restaurant championing Mid-Atlantic ingredients; starred every year since the DC guide launched in 2017 and a former Washingtonian #1.

    122 Blagden Alley NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, WASHINGTONIAN

  6. Must see · American, New American & Steak · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Oyster Oyster

    One Michelin star and a Michelin Green Star — Rob Rubba's vegetable-forward Shaw room; Rubba won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic (2023). Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.

    1440 8th St NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, JAMES BEARD

  7. Must see · Salvadoran, Mexican & Latin · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Causa

    One Michelin star — Carlos Delgado's upscale Peruvian in Blagden Alley (with casual Amazonia below); Delgado won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic (2025). Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.

    920 Blagden Alley NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, JAMES BEARD

  8. Must see · Mediterranean & Middle Eastern · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Maydan

    James Beard Award for Best New Restaurant (2018) — a soaring, live-fire Middle Eastern and North African room where everything meets an open wood fire; a Washingtonian 100 Very Best mainstay.

    1346 Florida Ave NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by JAMES BEARD, WASHINGTONIAN

  9. Must see · Chinese, Thai, Japanese & More · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Purple Patch

    Patrice Cleary's warm Mount Pleasant Filipino restaurant (2015) was named the Washington Post's Restaurant of the Year by Tom Sietsema in 2023 — his highest annual honor. The Southern Foodways Alliance and Positively Filipino have both told its story; a diaspora home-away-from-home for kare-kare, crispy lechon kawali and lumpia.

    3155 Mount Pleasant St NW, Washington, DC 20010

    Recommended by The Washington Post, SOUTHERNFOODWAYS

  10. Must see · Chinese, Thai, Japanese & More · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Tiger Fork

    A playful Hong Kong-style Cantonese spot tucked in Shaw's Blagden Alley with red lanterns and night-market energy — dim sum, cheung fun, chow fun and whole crispy fish. The Washington Post's Tom Sietsema ranked it #7 on his top-10 restaurants; Washingtonian and Time Out both praise it. Real Cantonese cooking inside the District.

    922 N St NW Rear, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by The Washington Post, WASHINGTONIAN

  11. Must see · Ethiopian & East African · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Letena

    Yamrot Ezineh's farm-to-table Ethiopian kitchen in Columbia Heights, spices imported from Ethiopia, standout vegetable dishes (sweet-savory carrot wat, deeply caramelized mushroom tibs) alongside berbere beef and braised-lamb yebeg wat. Named to Washingtonian's 100 Very Best Restaurants (2025) and to the Washington Post's best-Ethiopian roundup (2025).

    3100 14th St NW, Washington, DC 20010

    Recommended by WASHINGTONIAN, The Washington Post

  12. Worth the detour · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Lincoln Theatre

    A restored 1922 movie-and-vaudeville palace on 'Black Broadway,' where Duke Ellington, Ella Fitzgerald and Cab Calloway played, now a concert and event venue. A cornerstone of the U Street corridor's revival.

    Look for entertainment

    1215 U St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by Official site / operator, Destination DC (washington.org)

  13. Worth the detour · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Meridian Hill Park (Malcolm X Park)

    An Italianate terraced NPS park with the longest cascading fountain in North America and, on Sundays, a decades-old drum circle. Known locally as Malcolm X Park.

    Look for park

    2400 15th St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by National Park Service, Destination DC (washington.org)

  14. Worth the detour · Salvadoran, Mexican & Latin · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Gloria's Pupuseria

    A Columbia Heights hole-in-the-wall — Selena art on the walls, ranchera on the jukebox — turning out plump, well-stuffed pupusas with curtido for a couple dollars each. Repeatedly named among DC's best pupuserias; Salvadorans are the city's largest immigrant group and this is one of the canon rooms.

    3411 14th St NW, Washington, DC 20010

    Recommended by DCIST / WAMU, USA TODAY 10BEST

  15. Worth the detour · American, New American & Steak · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Rooster & Owl

    One Michelin star — chef Yuan Tang's four-course, choose-your-own-adventure menu on the 14th Street corridor, drawing from the Carolinas, Thailand, France and Japan. Retains its star in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.

    2436 14th St NW, Washington, DC 20009

    Recommended by MICHELIN STAR, Wikipedia

  16. Worth the detour · West & Sub-Saharan African · U Street, Shaw & Columbia Heights

    Appioo African Bar & Grill

    Chef Prince Matey's home-cooked Ghanaian mainstay in Shaw (2015), which Eater calls "Shaw's essential Ghanaian mainstay" for its stellar groundnut soup, egusi and jollof; Washingtonian folded it into its guide to DC's West African cooking. Live bands on weekends and a diaspora crowd — authentic West African, not a fusion approximation.

    1924 9th St NW, Washington, DC 20001

    Recommended by EATER DC, WASHINGTONIAN

Capitol Hill, H Street, Navy Yard & The Wharf 18

  1. Must see · Chinese, Thai, Japanese & More · Capitol Hill, H Street, Navy Yard & The Wharf

    Panda Gourmet

    The genuine-article Sichuan and Shaanxi kitchen hidden inside a Days Inn off New York Avenue NE. The Washington Post's $20 Diner said it "dazzles"; Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide calls it the best Chinese restaurant DC has ever had, with the best dan dan noodles the area has seen; Washington City Paper chronicled its cult following.

    2700 New York Ave NE, Washington, DC 20002

    Recommended by The Washington Post, TYLERCOWEN, WCP

  2. Must see · South Asian & Afghan · Capitol Hill, H Street, Navy Yard & The Wharf

    Daru

    Rasika alums Suresh Sundas and Dante Datta's low-lit "Indian-ish" bar-restaurant off H Street — tandoori lamb chops, black dal moored with burrata, inventive cocktails. In the MICHELIN Guide (2022), on the New York Times' 50 Best New Restaurants in America, and a Washingtonian 100 Very Best pick; The Infatuation is a fan.

    1451 Maryland Ave NE, Washington, DC 20002

    Recommended by WASHINGTONIAN, MICHELIN, DCIST / WAMU

  3. Must see · Capitol Hill, H Street, Navy Yard & The Wharf

    United States Capitol

    Sully Historic Site

    The 1794 home of Richard Bland Lee, Northern Virginia's first congressman and uncle of Robert E. Lee, preserved by the Fairfax County Park Authority beside Dulles Airport. Guided house tours plus a 'Forgotten Road' walking tour of the original outbuildings and enslaved-workers' quarters; grounds and trails are free.

75 sights and 59 places to eat from the National Mall out through Arlington to the Dulles corridor, each traceable to the source that named it. The monumental core — the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, the free Smithsonians, the Capitol — anchors the map; the food runs on what the region does best: the half-smoke at Ben’s, DC’s Ethiopian and Salvadoran kitchens, Chesapeake crab and oysters, the Michelin room and the Vietnamese sprawl of Eden Center.

How this guide was made

How the cuisine filters were policed

Every food card names a specific dish — a cuisine label alone doesn’t qualify. The region’s signature strengths are the half-smoke (Ben’s Chili Bowl), DC’s Ethiopian corridor along U Street, the area’s Salvadoran pupuserias, Chesapeake blue crab and oysters, the jumbo slice, and the Vietnamese sprawl of Eden Center — alongside a deep Michelin and James Beard fine-dining bench. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it happens to serve.

Web-searched, merit-measured and fact-checked

Every place is traceable to a credible source — Michelin, James Beard, Washingtonian, the Washington Post, Eater DC, Northern Virginia Magazine, ARLnow, the National Park Service and the Smithsonian — recorded in data/sources.json (direct map/page fetches are blocked in the build environment, so sources were confirmed via search). A mention is not merit: each place is measured for acclaim (award, rave, or a high rating with real volume) before it earns a pin. Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open.
